title: Secure node procurement and update walkthrough - Verdant Imaging
summary: Intro discovery to scope an on-prem, air-gapped Redwood private deployment for Verdant Imaging. Focus on hardware procurement constraints, offline update process, compliance (SOC2/ISO), and pilot timeline. AE + SE present; customer raised concerns about update signing, KMS in airgap, and required GPU types for inference. Agreed to share security pack, rough pricing, and a checklist for procurement and onsite procedures.
action_items: Alex Rivera - Send security pack (SOC2 + ISO artifacts) and draft pricing for dedicated/private options - due 2026-08-14
Priya Chen - Prepare a short runbook for offline update process (image signing, hashes, offline install steps) and sample verification script - due 2026-08-13
Mark Holloway - Share rack power spec (+ exact PDU layout) and preferred GPU SKUs (A100 or H100 candidates) - due 2026-08-10
Sofia Alvarez - Confirm whether HSM required or if customer-managed KMS behind airgap is acceptable - due 2026-08-12
next_steps: Redwood to send security pack + checklist
Customer to review procurement constraints and identify pilot cluster nodes
Schedule hands-on pilot kickoff week of 2026-08-24 (tentative)
Follow-up call to discuss signed update workflow and image delivery method
transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex Rivera: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro from our side, I'm Alex, AE on the account. Priya is our SE. how's it going?
[00:00:12] Mark Holloway: Hey Alex, good thanks. we, uh, are looking to replace a lot of our inference serving that's currently in cloud, but regs are pushing us on patient data residency so we need an on prem option.
[00:00:25] Priya Chen: Great, thanks Mark. can you give us a quick overview of the environment? network constraints, physical access, patch cadence?
[00:00:33] Mark Holloway: Sure. so the imaging center—3 racks, two of them available. 20U left, 16A circuits per rack, but power budget per rack is tight. we were thinking A100 80GB originally but Sofia's team is worried about heat and power.
[00:00:48] Sofia Alvarez: yeah, and also it's an isolated network. no outbound to internet. pretty much hermetic. updates have to be air-gapped, scanned, and signed by our security operations.
[00:00:57] Alex Rivera: Understood, that's typical for a lot of medtech. On the update side we support a signed-image workflow for Private that can be run offline—there's an image signing step and a verification tool. Priya will walk through specifics.
[00:01:08] Priya Chen: Quick note: we call it Redwood Private for the air-gapped install, it's the same runtime but packaged with an offline installer. Important bit—image signing uses our artifact signing tools, but we can also accept customer-signed manifests if you require full control.
[00:01:22] Tom Becker: So HSM required? Our auditors want KMS backed by FIPS HSM but in an airgap. is that doable?
[00:01:29] Priya Chen: Yes, there are two paths. one, you can have a customer-managed HSM inside the network and Redwood will integrate with it via the local KMS plugin. two, we can provide a sealed-off key delivery process and sign images in the cloud then ship them via secure thumb drive—though many customers prefer to manage keys themselves.
[00:01:44] Sofia Alvarez: We prefer local HSM. can't have private keys leave the facility.
[00:01:47] Alex Rivera: Noted. Priya, can you say a bit about encryption at rest and in transit inside the cluster?
[00:01:53] Priya Chen: Data at rest uses LUKS/dm-crypt for local volumes and we integrate with customer KMS for key material. In-transit between nodes is mTLS inside the cluster, and we support mutual TLS for any control plane traffic. small caveat: in an air-gapped mode the control plane runs locally, so logging and telemetry are optional by default and can be shipped out only via an approved process.
[00:02:10] Mark Holloway: okay. power's a hard stop for us though. we can do two x A100 80GB per node maybe but heat is a concern—our HVAC is not datacenter grade. any options for lower-TDP GPUs?
[00:02:20] Priya Chen: You can run with A10G or RTX6000 Ada in reduced throughput mode. there's also quantized model builds which reduce memory and compute and allow more cores per node. tradeoff is slightly lower throughput and sometimes quality delta. we can run a benchmark to show perf/quality tradeoffs.
[00:02:37] Tom Becker: how do you handle offline updates—like a monthly security patch? Do we need to take nodes down each time?
[00:02:44] Priya Chen: We support canary rollouts inside the private cluster. For air-gapped sites, update bundles are signed and delivered physically. The installer can do node-by-node rollout with zero-downtime for model runtime if you have a small fleet; otherwise schedule maintenance windows. We have a documented offline patch workflow—we'll share the runbook.
[00:03:02] Sofia Alvarez: Quick interruption—how do you ensure image provenance? we need deterministic hashes and an audit trail.
[00:03:09] Alex Rivera: Good question. Priya?
[00:03:11] Priya Chen: Images are hashed with SHA-256 and signatures are attached. we put metadata into the image manifest that contains build info and an immutable signing log. In private installs the manifest and the signature are verified locally before apply. The audit trail can be exported as a signed artifact for auditors.
[00:03:27] Mark Holloway: Awesome. procurement will want exact SKUs. Lina can you confirm what you need?
[00:03:31] Lina Park: yes, I'll need a short hardware spec and an approved vendor list. also lead times—GPUs are backordered right now so delivery dates matter.
[00:03:38] Alex Rivera: We'll include a procurement checklist—preferred GPUs, minimum memory, network endpoints, and power draw. We'll also include guidance for air-conditioned vs datacenter HVAC.
[00:03:47] Tom Becker: On the licensing side—do you charge per-token even in private? how does pricing differ for Private vs Dedicated?
[00:03:53] Alex Rivera: For Private deployments we typically do a platform licensing model—annual fee plus support, and optionally a per-throughput charge if you want Redwood to manage model hosting. Dedicated is reserved capacity in our cloud with usage pricing. We'll send a pricing matrix.
[00:04:05] Priya Chen: Also worth noting: you can bring your own model builds, or use Redwood-verified open models. For tightly-regulated clinics you often want deterministic model versions, so we recommend pinning a model version in the deployment config.
[00:04:16] Mark Holloway: What about benchmarking? we need throughput numbers for our job mix—mostly image-to-text inference, 512 tokens average.
[00:04:22] Priya Chen: We'll run a small benchmark with your sample workload. if you can provide a representative dataset (anonymized), we can test on A100 and a lower-TDP SKU to show latency and cost deltas.
[00:04:33] Tom Becker: timeline—if procurement moves quickly, can we be up for a pilot in 4-6 weeks?
[00:04:38] Alex Rivera: Potentially. Depends on lead times for hardware and contract approvals. We've seen pilots kick off in 3-8 weeks for similar customers.
[00:04:45] Sofia Alvarez: Also need SOC2 artifacts and penetration test reports. do you have those ready?
[00:04:50] Alex Rivera: Yes, we'll share our security pack. it includes SOC2 Type II report, ISO attestation, pen test summaries, and our standard isolation architecture diagrams.
[00:04:58] Mark Holloway: On the update delivery: you mentioned image on a thumb drive—how do we get chain-of-custody? auditors will want evidence.
[00:05:06] Priya Chen: We typically document a chain-of-custody process: signed manifests, tamper-evident packaging, and a scanned receipt upon hand-off. For HSM-backed signing inside your network, chain-of-custody is internal to you which most auditors prefer.
[00:05:17] Lina Park: procurement question — warranty and RMAs on the hardware if Redwood supplies nodes?
[00:05:21] Alex Rivera: If we coordinate hardware via a partner, we can put a support SLA in the contract that covers RMAs and spares. if you buy hardware directly we provide an integration and support layer but not hardware RMA management by default.
[00:05:33] Mark Holloway: Can we have a disconnected metrics export? we want to capture latency/volume but can't stream it out.
[00:05:39] Priya Chen: Absolutely—metrics can be stored locally and exported as a signed report. we also support a periodic manual export that your ops team can pull and ship to a secure analytics pipeline if needed.
[00:05:48] Tom Becker: Any known gotchas with Kubernetes in air-gapped mode? we run a minimal k8s distro but want to avoid heavy operators.
[00:05:55] Priya Chen: The private installer supports a minimal k8s or an orchestrator-less mode depending on your preference—some customers want systemd-managed services for simplicity. main gotchas are image pulls (must be pre-seeded) and cert rotation (need an offline rotation process). we'll include sample manifests.
[00:06:12] Mark Holloway: Good. about quantization—how risky is INT8 for our workloads?
[00:06:16] Priya Chen: INT8 is often fine for classification and many generation workloads but can have edge-case hallucination differences. we recommend a quick evaluation on a held-out set. sometimes mixed-precision (AMP) or 4-bit quantization with per-channel calibration yields the best perf/quality balance.
[00:06:32] Alex Rivera: I'd like to pause for a sec—any blockers that would prevent a pilot?
[00:06:36] Sofia Alvarez: we need to confirm HSM and procurement timelines. also agreement on who signs images.
[00:06:41] Lina Park: budget approvals by end of month would help.
[00:06:44] Alex Rivera: Understood. Priya and I will put together the documents. We'll aim to have the security pack and runbook by next week.
[00:06:51] [00:20:05] Priya Chen: (demo note) When we do an offline install, the install bundle includes a pre-verified runtime tarball. The verification script checks the signature and then unpacks into the runtime dir. If verification fails the installer aborts; logs are written locally and a signed audit artifact is created.
[00:20:42] Mark Holloway: sounds good, how do you handle rollback?
[00:20:46] Priya Chen: We keep previous signed bundles and the installer supports node-level rollback to last-known-good. We also support canarying—so you can roll to 1 node then promote.
[00:21:10] Tom Becker: about the model updates—if we want to retrain in-house and deploy new model artifacts, how do we push those?
[00:21:16] Priya Chen: Model artifacts are just another signed bundle. You can sign them with your key and upload to the local artifact store. Redwood runtime will verify signature before loading. this avoids needing to ship models out.
[00:21:30] Mark Holloway: ok. procurement will also want installation scope—do you do onsite install?
[00:21:35] Alex Rivera: We offer an onsite onboarding service as an add-on—engineers will come in to complete initial install and hand over runbooks. Many regulated customers choose that.
[00:21:43] Lina Park: budget for onsite is fine if it shortens time to live.
[00:21:47] Sofia Alvarez: small nit—do you log raw patient data anywhere in plaintext?
[00:21:52] Priya Chen: No. We don't persist PII. models see the inputs in memory, but persistent logs are redacted by default. Any export is under your control and redaction policies are configurable.
[00:21:59] Mark Holloway: good.
[00:22:03] [00:35:10] Alex Rivera: let's recap next steps. We'll send: security pack, procurement checklist with SKUs and power, offline update runbook, and a sample benchmark plan.
[00:35:22] Priya Chen: I'll also draft a short script you can run locally to verify signatures and produce an audit artifact.
[00:35:28] Lina Park: and I'll try to get GPU lead times by Friday.
[00:35:33] Tom Becker: let's tentatively plan a pilot kick-off week of Aug 24 pending hardware.
[00:35:39] Alex Rivera: Perfect. Any last questions?
[00:35:43] Sofia Alvarez: Could you add a note about our requirement for FIPS 140-2 HSM certs in the pack?
[00:35:49] Alex Rivera: We'll include that.
[00:35:52] Mark Holloway: thanks all.
[00:35:54] Alex Rivera: Thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the next call.
[00:36:05] [End of recording - actual duration ~52 minutes]
